comb-crunch.notes: 'Graham Cracker Steps': close-field stereo recording (Zoom H4n + AKG Perception) of graham crackers crushed one at a time, described by the author as usable as footsteps. Nine isolated crumbles about 1.1 s apart; six used (0.19-0.30 s), chosen for similar level. Dry, crisp and crumbly, no mouth sounds, noise floor about -68 dBFS, no clipping. Substitute texture: a cracker crumble stands in for brittle honeycomb candy (no CC0 honeycomb or dalgona recording turned up; eating recordings were all mouth noise). The raw crumble is bright (centroid 3.3-6.0 kHz, 25-50% of the energy above 5 kHz), so a -3 dB high shelf above 6 kHz was applied; centroid is now 2.8-4.9 kHz. Listen for first: whether it still sounds too sizzly; if so a steeper shelf or a low-pass can be applied to these files.

sources.title: Sticky Footsteps + door opening with beeping sound.
sources.author: SteeLManure

honey-stick.notes: 'Sticky Footsteps': the author walks in shoes on a very sticky floor; each step is a heel strike followed by the sticky 'tack' of the sole peeling off, which is the foot-unsticking sound wanted here. Six single steps (0.12-0.19 s) from the first 17 s, before the door and beep at the end of the file. Centroid 1.6-3.4 kHz. Weakest recording technically: noise floor about -53 dBFS (the limit is -50), so slices carry +10 to +15 dB of gain and the hiss floor is audible in the tails. Substitute texture: sticky shoe-sole peel instead of honey. No better CC0 'sticky peel' was found: tape peels and rips were 5-7 kHz and clipped, plunger and suction pops were 300 Hz thumps or tiny ticks, and a second sticky-floor recording was too noisy (-41 dBFS).

drop-squish.notes: 'Squishy Foot Steps': squeezes of a squishy fidget toy recorded as jelly-creature footsteps (44.1 kHz/24-bit stereo, noise floor about -74 dBFS, no clipping). Seven squeezes in 2.5 s; six used, and the seventh, a dense one 4-5 dB louder than the rest, was dropped. Slices are 0.07-0.15 s soft wet squeezes with fine popping texture (centroid 1.8-4.4 kHz), no gore and no voice. It reads more as a squeeze than a clean soft 'tok'. Only six clean events exist, so this is the minimum count, and the shortest slice (0.069 s) is close to the 0.06 s floor.

wood-tap.notes: 'Sticks Hitting sticks': wooden sticks knocked together ('dull wood sounds'), 48 kHz/16-bit stereo, noise floor about -69 dBFS, no clipping. Nine single knocks of 0.07-0.11 s with a woody resonance between 0.74 and 1.65 kHz and a fast decay, and almost nothing above 5 kHz. Chosen over woodblock and claves recordings, which are almost pure tones at 2.3-2.6 kHz (over 93% of the energy in the 2-5 kHz band) and therefore a piercing risk, and over finger and pencil taps, which were clicky and noisy. The resonance pitch differs a little between slices, so random picks will vary slightly in pitch; that reads like different taps on a stick.

honey-loop.notes: 'gunk bubbling in cave': per the description a small fountain pitched down with reverb added (Zoom H4n Pro XY, 44.1 kHz/16-bit stereo, L/R correlation 0.40, so the stereo image is kept). Slow, soft, thick bubbling and gloops with a warm spectrum: centroid about 0.75 kHz and essentially nothing above 3 kHz. It is the closest 'slow viscous drip' texture found; there is no CC0 honey or syrup drip recording of usable quality (thick-liquid, oil-pour and mud recordings were glugging, bassy under 500 Hz, or noisy). The 3.95 s loop (52.15-56.25 s of the file, the last 150 ms being the crossfade tail) has a calm seam (level around the join matches the loop average within 1 dB); level swings by about 7 dB between 250 ms steps and the loudest 50 ms is 11 dB above the median, which is the bigger gloops of the bubbling itself. Substitute texture: pitched-down water, not real honey. Mostly below 2 kHz, so it will be quiet on laptop speakers; raise its playback gain in the game rather than its normalization.
